findings.claim: FileStore::write joins an untrusted, wire-supplied key directly onto the store root with no canonicalization or component filtering, and additionally calls create_dir_all on the resulting parent, so a key such as '../../../home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys' or an absolute path like '/etc/cron.d/evil' (Path::join discards the root entirely when the joined component is absolute) lets an attacker create directories and write attacker-controlled bytes anywhere the process user can write, escaping the store root and reaching code-execution paths.
findings.proposedReproduction: let s = FileStore::new("/tmp/store".into()).unwrap(); s.write("../../../tmp/pwned", b"x").unwrap(); assert!(std::path::Path::new("/tmp/pwned").exists()); and s.write("/tmp/abs_pwned", b"x") writes outside root via absolute-path join

findings.claim: FileStore::read joins the untrusted key onto the store root without sanitization (the doc comment on line 19 states keys arrive from the wire untrusted), so a key of '../../etc/passwd' or an absolute path reads arbitrary files outside the store root; status_response then leaks the result back to the caller as the file's byte length, giving an attacker a file-existence and size oracle over the whole filesystem.
findings.proposedReproduction: FileStore::new("/tmp/store".into()).unwrap().read("../../etc/passwd") returns the contents of /etc/passwd instead of erroring

findings.claim: The 'put' arm of handle_request unwraps directly on untrusted wire input at three points: parts.next().unwrap() for the key, parts.next().unwrap() for the TTL, and .parse().unwrap() on the TTL string. Any remote request of the form 'put', 'put:k', or 'put:k:abc' panics the request handler, letting an unauthenticated attacker terminate the process with a single short request — the 'get' arm shows the intended None-handling that this arm omits.
findings.proposedReproduction: handle_request(&mut Cache::new(8), "put") panics on unwrap of None; handle_request(&mut Cache::new(8), "put:k:notanumber") panics on parse().unwrap()

findings.claim: SharedCounter::read_or_init acquires and releases the mutex three separate times instead of holding one guard across the check-then-use, so the contains_key result is stale by the time the second lock is taken; a concurrent SharedCounter::remove of the same key between the two acquisitions makes .get(key).unwrap() return None and panic, so an attacker able to drive concurrent counter removal (e.g. a request that removes a counter while another reads it) can crash the process on demand.
findings.proposedReproduction: Thread A loops read_or_init("k") while thread B loops remove("k"); the interleaving where B removes between A's contains_key and A's get panics on unwrap of None

findings.claim: Cache::put pushes the key onto the `order` deque on every call but only inserts into `map`, so repeated puts of the same attacker-chosen key leave map.len() at 1 — never reaching the max_entries eviction trigger — while `order` grows by one owned String per request without bound. An attacker replaying 'put:k:1' drives unbounded heap growth and exhausts memory, defeating the stated bounded-memory guarantee.
findings.proposedReproduction: let mut c = Cache::new(64); for _ in 0..1_000_000 { c.put("k".repeat(1000), "v".into()) } — c.len() stays 1 while the internal order deque holds 1,000,000 keys (~1GB)
